name: Stalemate and other draws
goal: You can avoid stalemate when you are winning, aim for it when you are losing, and know the other draws: repetition and too little material to mate.
intro: Not every game ends in mate. Stalemate is a draw: the player to move is not in check but has no legal move. A game is also drawn when the same position comes up three times with the same player to move, and when neither side has enough pieces left to give mate, such as king against king, or king and knight against king. When you are winning, these rules are traps to avoid; when you are losing, they can save half a point.

parts.title: Mate, not stalemate
parts.keyIdea: Against a lone king, check before every move that it will still have a legal move, unless your move is mate.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess: White has a queen against a lone king, and Black's king is stuck near the corner. A move later, White in the game played a natural-looking queen move and only drew. Find the mate instead.

notes.text: Your king comes closer, so that it can protect the queen on b7 next move. Black's king still has a8 to go to, so this is not stalemate.

Mate: the queen checks from b7, and your king on c6 guards it, so Black's king cannot take it. In the game White played Qb6 here instead. That gave no check, but it took away a7, b7 and b8, so Black's king had no legal move left: stalemate, and the game was drawn.

parts.title: Stalemate to the rescue
parts.keyIdea: If your king has no legal moves, giving away your last piece can force stalemate and save a lost game.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess: you have only a rook against a queen, which is normally lost. Your king is in check. Look at how many squares it will have left after this move, and think about what that could mean.

notes.text: The only legal move. Now your king has no squares at all: Black's queen covers f1, f2, g2 and h1, and your rook stands on h2. Only the rook can still move.

Black's king has just attacked your rook, and the rook answers with a check right next to it. If Black takes it, with the king or with the queen, you have no legal move and you are not in check: stalemate. In the game Black took with the king, and it was a draw.

parts.title: Too little to mate
parts.keyIdea: When you are losing, trading off the last pieces can leave too little material to mate, which is a draw.
parts.text: A Lichess Puzzle: Black has a queen and a pawn against your rook, and the pawn is about to give check. You are losing, but remember the third kind of draw: with only the two kings left, nobody can give mate.

notes.text: The rook takes the pawn with check, and from f3 it also attacks Black's queen on c3 along the third rank. If Black's king steps away, you take the queen, so Black's best is to take your rook.
Black's queen took your rook, and your king takes the queen. Only the two kings are left, so neither side can ever give mate, and the game is a draw at once.
